title: Useful and harmful physical and chemical changes
competency: Identify useful and harmful physical and chemical changes in everyday life.

keywords.def: A change in physical appearance, not in chemical composition. No new substance forms.
A change in chemical composition. New substances form.
The chemical change in plants that makes food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.

en.text: Physical changes help us: evaporation and condensation make the water cycle, freezing preserves food, and melting and bending make tools. Cutting trees and oil spills are harmful physical changes. Photosynthesis, cooking, digestion, fermentation and burning fuel are useful chemical changes. Rusting, souring food, smoke and dumped chemicals are harmful.

screens.title: Injera batter
screens.ask: Making injera needs the batter to ferment. Is fermentation useful or harmful here?
screens.after:
Useful. Fermentation is a chemical change: yeast forms new substances in the batter.
It gives injera its sour taste and soft holes.
The same useful change makes bread and tella.

screens.title: Useful physical changes
paras: Evaporation and condensation create the water cycle.
Freezing preserves food, medicine and other materials.
Melting, cutting, bending and moulding make tools.
We mix substances, and we separate them from mixtures.

screens.title: Harmful physical changes
paras: Examples: cutting trees, bad weather, oil spills.

screens.title: Useful chemical changes
paras: Photosynthesis in plants makes the food we depend on.
Most energy we use comes from chemical changes, released as heat or electricity.
Making food and medicine, digestion, fermentation and cooking are useful chemical changes.

screens.title: Harmful chemical changes
paras: Rusting of cars, bridges and ships.
Souring of food, burning of fuel and smoke.
Plastic disposal and dumping of chemicals.

root.label: Changes around us
root.info: Changes are physical or chemical. Each kind can be useful or harmful.

screens.title: Key words
defs: The chemical change in plants that makes food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.

screens.text: Which of these is a useful chemical change?
opts: Souring of milk you wanted fresh
screens.why:
Step 1: which ones are chemical? Rusting, cooking and souring form new substances. An oil spill is physical.
Step 2: which helps us? Cooking makes food safe and tasty.
Rusting damages bridges, and souring spoils milk: harmful.
So cooking food is the useful chemical change.

items: Evaporation and condensation give us rain.
The oil only spreads over the water, but it harms fish and birds.
Food is broken into new substances our body uses.
Rust is new and weakens the car.
Cold keeps meat fresh; it is still meat.
Burning forms new gases that pollute the air.
screens.why:
Step 1: does a new substance form? No → physical. Yes → chemical.
Step 2: does it help us or harm us?
Water cycle and freezing meat: useful physical. Oil spill: harmful physical.
Digestion: useful chemical. Rusting and smoke: harmful chemical.
screens.clue: Does it form something new? Does it help us?
screens.text: Sort each change into one of four groups: useful or harmful, physical or chemical.
True or false? Cutting trees is a harmful physical change.
screens.why:
Cutting changes only the size and shape of the wood. No new substance forms: physical.
The book lists cutting trees as harmful: forests and soil are lost.
So the statement is true.
screens.clue: Does cutting form a new substance?

screens.text: Stop a harmful change: painting an iron gate stops it from rusting. Why does this help?
opts: It stops a harmful chemical change by keeping air and water away
Paint is a physical change that makes rust
screens.ans: It stops a harmful chemical change by keeping air and water away
screens.why:
Rusting is a harmful chemical change.
In Experiment 2.3, iron rusted in water that contained air.
Paint covers the iron and keeps air and water away.
No air and water → no rust. The gate is still iron, not a non-metal.
screens.clue: What did the nail need in Experiment 2.3 to rust?

items.title: I Q1. Physical or chemical? (a–e)
items: b. Food with saliva and digestive enzymes
Digestion breaks food into new substances.
c. Potassium reacting with water to give hydrogen
Hydrogen gas is a new substance.
d. Straightening bent iron with a hammer
Only the shape of the iron changes.
Burning forms ash, smoke and gases.
items.why:
Ask: does a new substance form?
a and d: wood is still wood, iron is still iron → physical.
b: enzymes break food into new substances → chemical.
c: potassium and water form hydrogen gas, a new substance → chemical.
e: a burning match forms ash and smoke → chemical.
items.text: Exercise 2.7 I Q1: classify each change as physical or chemical.

items.title: I Q1. Physical or chemical? (f–i)
items: Plants make food and oxygen: new substances.
Cooking changes the egg; it cannot be reversed.
The salt can be got back by evaporation.
items.why:
f: photosynthesis makes food and oxygen, new substances → chemical.
g: a boiled egg cannot become raw again → chemical.
h: boiling water turns it into steam, still water → physical.
i: dissolved salt is recovered by evaporation → physical.
items.text: Exercise 2.7 I Q1: classify each change as physical or chemical.
Name the kind of change: a change in size, shape and state of a substance is a ___
items.why:
Size, shape and state are physical properties.
Changing them forms no new substance.
So it is a physical change. "Cyclic change" is not one of the two kinds in the book.

items.text: Physical or chemical? Which of the following statements is correct?
opts: Digestion of food is a chemical change
Burning of paper is a physical change
items.ans: Digestion of food is a chemical change
items.why:
Evaporation: water becomes vapour, still water → physical. So the first is wrong.
Burning paper: ash and gases form → chemical. So the third is wrong.
Digestion: food is broken into new substances → chemical. Correct.
So "All" is wrong too.

items.text: Among the following, which one is a physical change?
items.why:
Burning a candle forms carbon dioxide and water vapour: chemical.
Fermentation forms alcohol and carbon dioxide: chemical.
A magnetised iron bar is still iron: physical.
So the answer is making an iron bar magnetic.

items: Spoiled food has new substances and a bad smell.
Wax burns to carbon dioxide and water vapour.
items.why:
Ask: does a new substance form?
Chemical (new substances): burning charcoal, fermentation, rusting, spoilage of food, burning candle.
Physical (same substance): melting ice, dissolving sugar, evaporation of water.
items.text: Activity 2.13: classify each change as physical or chemical.

test.text: Which of these is a useful physical change?
test.why:
Rusting, smoke and food spoilage form new substances: chemical, and harmful.
Freezing only changes the state of the food: physical.
It keeps food fresh, so it is useful.

test.text: True or false? Rusting of ships and bridges is a harmful chemical change.
test.why:
Rust is a new substance, so rusting is chemical.
It weakens ships and bridges, so it is harmful.
The book lists it as a harmful chemical change. True.

Plants make food (sugar) and oxygen: new substances → chemical.
Plants and we depend on this food → useful.
So photosynthesis is a useful chemical change.

test.text: Which of these is a harmful physical change?
test.why:
Fermentation and cooking are chemical changes.
The water cycle is physical but useful.
An oil spill: the oil only spreads (physical), but it harms water life.
So an oil spill is the harmful physical change.

test.text: Find the pair: which pair is "useful chemical change, harmful chemical change"?
test.why:
Cooking food: new substances, helps us → useful chemical.
Dumping chemicals: pollutes land and water → harmful chemical.
Melting ice, cutting trees and freezing food are physical, so the other pairs fail.
Rusting is harmful and fermentation useful: that pair is in the wrong order.
